name: Jamie Dimon

summary.text: Jamie Dimon is the chief executive of JPMorgan Chase. In 2012 the bank's Chief Investment Office lost more than $6 billion on synthetic credit derivatives (the 'London Whale' trades). A March 2013 Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations report found that the bank mischaracterised high-risk trading as hedging, mismarked positions, manipulated risk models and misinformed regulators and investors; Dimon had described the early reports of losses as a 'tempest in a teapot' on an April 2012 earnings call and later told a Senate committee he had been 'dead wrong'. In September 2013 JPMorgan paid $920 million to U.S. and U.K. regulators, including $200 million to the SEC, and admitted the facts underlying the SEC's charges.

facts.claim: On an April 13, 2012 earnings call Dimon described press reports about the Chief Investment Office's London trading losses as a 'tempest in a teapot'; the Senate subcommittee later found the bank had ignored internal alarms weeks and in some cases months earlier.
facts.quote: Dimon described the London trading losses as a "tempest in a teapot" on an April 13, 2012 earnings conference call

facts.claim: Testifying before the Senate Banking Committee in June 2012, Dimon said of his 'tempest in a teapot' remark: 'When I made that statement, I was dead wrong,' adding that he had been assured by his lieutenants that the problem was an isolated incident.
facts.quote: When I made that statement, I was dead wrong.

sources.title: Senate treats JPMorgan CEO Dimon with kid gloves

facts.claim: The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations' March 2013 report concluded that JPMorgan 'mischaracterized high-risk trading as hedging', mismarked its trading book to hide losses, manipulated risk models and withheld key information from its primary regulator, in some instances at Dimon's behest. These are the subcommittee's findings, not a court ruling.

facts.claim: The subcommittee's investigation found that the Chief Investment Office used its Synthetic Credit Portfolio for high-risk trading, mismarked the trading book to hide losses, manipulated risk models, dodged regulatory oversight and misinformed outside parties about the trades; Carl Levin chaired the subcommittee and John McCain was ranking member.

facts.claim: In September 2013 JPMorgan agreed to pay about $920 million in penalties to the SEC, the Federal Reserve, the OCC and the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority over the London Whale trades, including a $200 million SEC penalty, and admitted the facts underlying the SEC's charges and that it violated the federal securities laws.
facts.quote: JPMorgan has agreed to settle the SEC's charges by paying a $200 million penalty, admitting the facts underlying the SEC's charges, and publicly acknowledging that it violated the federal securities laws.

facts.claim: The SEC's 2013 settlement with JPMorgan was among the first under the agency's revised policy of requiring admissions of wrongdoing in some cases; the admitted facts supported violations of Sections 13(a), 13(b)(2)(A) and 13(b)(2)(B) of the Exchange Act and Rules 13a-11, 13a-13 and 13a-15.

openQuestions: Site claim that Dimon 'famously dismissed the Whale's losses as a tempest in a teapot': supported (Bloomberg report on the Senate subcommittee findings; Dimon's own June 2012 Senate testimony).

Site claims that the CIO held about $350 billion in excess deposits, that the Synthetic Credit Portfolio reached about $157 billion notional, and that a January 2012 VaR model change cut reported VaR by about 50%: not tested here; the full Senate report text should be checked for these figures.
Site claim that hedge funds BlueMountain and Saba traded against the position: not covered by any source returned.
Site figure of $6.2 billion in trading losses and 'over $1 billion' in fines: the $920 million regulatory total is documented; the $6.2 billion figure was not confirmed here.
When Dimon became CEO and chairman of JPMorgan Chase was not confirmed from a primary source.
